title: Stock picking multi-tier system built with just a basic llm subscription, free tier connectors. Looking for feedback.
author: lestwemeetagain
selftext:
Been chatting with the llms to get lucky who came up with this system. Not paying for anything other than the entry level llm subscription. The connectors are free tier, hence limited.

**The System:**

Every stock has to clear 4 hard cutoffs first: decent growth, controlled risk/leverage, big enough to trade easily, and clean accounting (that last one isn't fully live yet). Fail any one and it's out, no exceptions.

Whatever survives gets scored on 7 things: valuation, momentum/positioning, analyst backing, management quality, upcoming catalysts, growth durability, and sector timing. Each is worth +1, 0, or -1, valuation counts double. Add it up and that's the rank.

Fair value itself is just a formula, not a guess: take the analyst price target, discount it 15% for optimism bias, discount it further if the stock's already fallen a lot. No cherry-picking, same math for every name.

**How it actually runs:**

Everything lives inside a Project so nothing resets between sessions, snapshots and methodology notes get saved there as I go. For a full rerun across 40+ names the llm spins up 4 to 6 parallel AI subagents to pull live prices, sentiment and macro data instead of doing it one ticker at a time. It's plugged into a dozen-ish data source tools, though only two of them actually earned a permanent spot in the system. Final tables land in Google Sheets.

Tell me why this is stupid. I built it to stop myself from doing dumb shit and I fully expect this sub to find the one loophole that lets me do dumb shit anyway.

[](https://www.reddit.com/submit/?source_id=t3_1wdy3f1&composer_entry=crosspost_prompt)

comments.author: TopPromise9775
comments.body:
Disclosure: I build a tool in this space (ForecastNest), so discount accordingly.

  
The loophole you asked for: your fair value is an anchor, not an estimate. "Analyst PT minus 15%" means the model never independently forms a view — it inherits sell-side consensus and applies a constant you picked. And LLMs anchor hard on numbers you hand them.

  
We once mistyped a baseline and told five models an ETF trading near $760 was at $1.00. Our prompt did instruct them to anchor to the given baseline, in fairness — three of them built careful, hedged ranges around a dollar anyway. Two ignored the instruction and priced the real asset.

  
So the 15% haircut isn't correcting optimism bias. It's relocating it.

  
Second thing: nothing in your pipeline closes the loop. You rank 40 names, the sheet updates, and then what? If the ranks aren't stamped at the time and checked against what actually happened later, you can't tell whether the system stops you doing dumb shit or just gives the dumb shit a score. That's the part everyone skips, and it's the only part that eventually tells you whether any of those seven factors carry information.

replies.author: lestwemeetagain
replies.body:
Both fair hits, honestly.

On the haircut: you're right, it's not an independent estimate, it's consensus with a discount slapped on. Calling it a "correction for optimism bias" oversells it, it's really just a margin of safety on top of someone else's number, and if consensus is wrong in a specific direction, the 15% doesn't know that, it just makes the wrong number slightly less wrong. Should've called it a safety margin from the start instead of pretending it's independently derived.

On closing the loop, no argument at all, that's already sitting in my own "what's missing" notes and I haven't fixed it yet. No timestamped rank log means I genuinely don't know if any of the seven factors carry information or if I'm just watching myself confirm what I already wanted to buy. That's the actual next build, not another gate, a dated log of every rank plus forward 1/3/6/12mo returns per name. Until that exists everything above it is a nice looking guess with extra steps.
